title: Data Science Project: Predicting Prices of Diamond using dataset from R library
text: This dataset contains the prices and other attributes of almost 54,000 diamonds. The dataset is used to predict the price of a diamond based on its characteristics such as carat, cut, color, clarity, and dimensions. The project involves data cleaning, exploratory data analysis, and building predictive models to understand the factors that influence diamond prices. The goal is to create a model that can accurately predict the price of a diamond based on its attributes.

text:
Correlation Table

num_vars <- diamonds %>% select(price, carat, x, y, z)
cor_table <- cor(num_vars)
corrplot(cor_table, method = 'number')








Only numerical variables are used for correlation matrix. It makes sense that carat is highly correlated with x, y and z: the bigger the diamond the heavier. The most interesting observation here is the high correlation between price and carat.

Modelling

Both Linear Regression and Random Forest are used to compare the accuracy of the predictions.
log_price and log_carat were used in the linear regression model whereas Random Forest used variables without conversion. This is due to Linear Regression assumeing linearity and constant variance.
Random Forest, on the other hand, handles skewed distribution and heteroscedasticity much better. It is easier to interpret raw data.
Both of these exclude variables such as x, y, z etc. as they are variables strongly related to each other. Including them in these models may lead to multicollinearity and the over-fitting of the data.

rmse_lm <- rmse(obs, pred)

rmse_lm; r2_lm

[1] 792.1002


[1] 0.9607776


log() was transformed back to the raw data with exp().
Although the lines shown on these graphs are straight, the dots spread out as higher the price becomes. The higher the price becomes, more errors in prediction becomes obvious. The increase in values of residuals is visible, therefore the conclusions are that:

Linear regression assumption of constant variance are not met
Model predictions are less reliable for more expensive diamonds as errors are larger

Despite these results, the residuals are small for typical diamonds, so the linear regression model predicts well in the common price range.
Random Forest handles this better because it does not assume constant variance.

title: Hypertension Clinical Treatment Analysis
text: This dataset was taken from: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/isabelladil/phase-iii-clinical-trial-dataset/data It is a synthetic data and does not contain any data of individuals in real life.

title: Hypertension Clinical Treatment Analysis
text:
Study Design and Dataset
This study used a synthetic clinical trial dataset consisting of 1,000 patients enrolled across multiple study sites. Each patient record included demographic variables (age, gender), clinical measurements (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, cholesterol level), treatment allocation, adverse event counts, and dropout status. Three treatment groups were evaluated: Drug A (CardioX), Drug B (active comparator), and Placebo.

title: Hypertension Clinical Treatment Analysis
text:
Data Preparation and Cleaning
Missing data: Checked using colSums(is.na()); no missing values were present.
Outliers: Potential outliers in cholesterol levels were identified using the IQR method within age-stratified groups to avoid age-related confounding.
Age grouping: Patients were categorised into four age groups (6–19, 20–39, 40–59, 60–98 years) using the cut() function to support visualisation and subgroup comparisons.
A binary variable hypertension was created to classify patients based on commonly accepted thresholds (≥140 mmHg systolic or ≥90 mmHg diastolic), reflecting individuals likely in need of treatment.

title: Hypertension Clinical Treatment Analysis
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
Descriptive statistics and graphical visualisations (bar charts, histograms, scatterplots, and boxplots) were generated using the tidyverse and ggplot2 packages. These visualisations were used to: - Assess treatment group balance - Evaluate distributions of age, blood pressure, and cholesterol - Examine relationships between age, cholesterol level, and blood pressure - Compare blood pressure outcomes across treatment groups - Explore dropout patterns

title: Hypertension Clinical Treatment Analysis
text:
Statistical Analysis

Group Comparisons
Because blood pressure values were not assumed to be normally distributed, non-parametric tests were used: - Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied to compare systolic and diastolic blood pressure across the three treatment groups. - Pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction were used for post-hoc comparisons.


Categorical Outcomes
To compare the proportion of patients with hypertension across treatment groups, a Chi-squared test was conducted using a contingency table of hypertension status by treatment group.


Predictors of Persistent Hypertension
A multivariable logistic regression model was fitted to identify factors associated with remaining hypertensive after treatment. Predictors included: - Treatment group - Age - Gender - Cholesterol level - Number of adverse events
The model was fitted using the glm() function with a binomial link. Multicollinearity was assessed using Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) via the car::vif() function.


Software
All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.2). Key libraries included tidyverse, ggplot2, rstatix, and car.

Interpretation (Clinical Context)
It is very important to keep in mind that these are all real-life data with many missing values and errors. It is not possible to know where there may be errors, but a few possibilities include:

Error submitting an update as a new case
Entry error
Multiple drug administration by one patient leading to identifying the wrong drug as the culprit of adverse reactions

While there are many possible errors to keep in mind, the data has a huge number of cases reported. The bigger the data the clearer the consistency and the more accurate the analysis becomes. An increase in reports however does not necessarily indicate increased risk. Possible contributors include:

Increased prescribing
Media attention
Regulatory changes

The results should be read and analysed with the potential errors and influences in mind, and any healthcare professionals or researchers who intend to use this as reference should always use their clinical judgement.

Hi, I’m Reina, the founder of Reina’s Data Studio.
I help researchers, students, technical teams, healthcare professionals and many others work with data clearly, ethically, and confidently using R.



Why I started Reina’s Data Studio
I have always wanted to build a career using R — a language I genuinely enjoy and believe is incredibly powerful, especially for healthcare and research. In reality, R-focused roles are still relatively uncommon, and I reached a point where continuing to search for another traditional role felt limiting rather than motivating.
I also realised that I work best when I can focus on helping others, working independently, and sharing what I know — rather than working under rigid structures that don’t align with how I do my best work.
Starting Reina’s Data Studio gave me the freedom to do exactly that:
to support people working with real data, and to show how effective and enjoyable R can be when used thoughtfully.


My background
My professional journey began in pharmacy, where accuracy, responsibility, and understanding the meaning behind data are essential. Over time, I realised that what I enjoyed most was analysing information and solving problems — which led me to computer science and data science.
I studied computer science with a data science focus, where R became my primary tool. I later worked in system engineering to gain broader technical experience, but my long-term goal was always to work directly with data.
Resigning from my system engineering role became a turning point — one that pushed me to fully commit to building a data-focused career on my own terms. Reina’s Data Studio is the result of that decision.


How my healthcare background shapes my work
Coming from pharmacy means I don’t treat data as abstract numbers.
I understand:

Where healthcare and research data comes from
What each variable represents
Why accuracy, consistency, and assumptions matter

This allows me to approach analysis with precision and context, not just technical skill. It also means I’m especially careful about ethics, privacy, and reproducibility — all of which are critical when working with sensitive data.


How I work with clients
Clients often describe my working style as:

Calm and detail-oriented
Collaborative and supportive
Clear and honest

I’m not afraid to ask questions — because understanding your goals properly is the fastest way to deliver work you can trust. I adapt to each client’s working style and aim for 100% clarity and satisfaction, whether that means detailed explanations or straightforward results.
Trust is central to everything I do. I want clients to feel safe sharing their data and confident in the work we produce together.


Values that guide my work

Transparency — clear communication, no unnecessary complexity
Passion for data — curiosity and care in every project
Education & continuous learning — knowledge grows, and so should we

These values shape both my consulting work and my teaching.


Teaching and knowledge sharing
Learning has always been a core part of my life. I truly believe that knowledge never betrays, and that learning should feel empowering — even fun.
Through YouTube tutorials, mentoring, and teaching, I share practical R knowledge so others can work more confidently with data. R is constantly evolving, and I enjoy growing alongside it while helping others do the same.


Language support
I provide support in English and Japanese.
Because many R resources are only available in English, I especially enjoy helping Japanese speakers who may be struggling with language barriers before they even get to the programming itself.


Who I work best with
I work best with people who value:

Mutual respect
Collaboration
Thoughtful, ethical data work

Projects that involve disrespectful communication or a lack of cooperation are not a good fit for my approach.


Let’s work together
If you have a dataset, question, or project in mind, I’d love to hear from you.
You don’t need to have everything figured out — we can work through it together.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
text:
Healthcare data is not just data.
Behind every dataset are real patients, real decisions, and real consequences. A misplaced assumption or undocumented change is not simply a technical issue — it can affect interpretation, policy, or treatment decisions.
That is why reproducibility is not optional in healthcare data analysis. It is foundational.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
text:
What Does “Reproducibility” Actually Mean?
In simple terms, reproducibility means:

If someone else runs your analysis using the same data and code, they should get the same results.

That sounds obvious. But in practice, it is surprisingly easy to break reproducibility.
Common issues include:

Manual data edits in Excel
Copy-pasted results without saved code
Untracked changes to datasets
Hard-coded values with no explanation
Analyses run interactively without documentation

In research and healthcare settings, these small shortcuts accumulate into serious risk.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
section: Why It Matters More in Healthcare
text:
Why It Matters More in Healthcare
In some industries, minor inconsistencies might be inconvenient.
In healthcare, they can be dangerous.
Reproducibility matters because:

1. Accuracy and Accountability
Healthcare decisions often rely on statistical outputs. If results cannot be traced back to documented steps, confidence in those results weakens.
Reproducible workflows create an audit trail:

What data was used?
What cleaning steps were applied?
What assumptions were made?
What model was fitted?

This level of clarity protects both patients and professionals.


2. Transparency for Collaboration
Clinical and research projects rarely involve just one person. Analysts, clinicians, reviewers, and stakeholders may all interact with the results.
When analysis is reproducible:

Team members can verify findings
Assumptions can be discussed openly
Changes can be implemented systematically

Without reproducibility, collaboration becomes fragile and dependent on memory rather than structure.


3. Long-Term Sustainability
Healthcare research often spans months or years.
If you revisit a project six months later and cannot easily regenerate the results, you lose time and confidence.
Reproducible workflows mean:

You can re-run the analysis with updated data
You can adjust models without starting from scratch
You can respond to reviewer comments efficiently

This is not just about neatness. It is about sustainability.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
text:
How R Supports Reproducibility
One of the reasons I chose R is its ability to create a beautiful reproducible analysis.
Tools such as:

R Markdown
Quarto
Structured project folders
Script-based data cleaning

allow analysis, interpretation, and reporting to exist in a single, transparent workflow.
Instead of:

Clean data manually
Run analysis
Copy results into a Word document

all using separate programs,
You can:

Clean data using documented scripts
Run statistical models in code
Generate reports automatically

The entire process becomes traceable and repeatable, because the entire process is saved in one big tool.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
text:
A Practical Example
Imagine analysing a clinical dataset comparing treatment groups.
Without reproducibility:

Data cleaning happens in Excel
Outliers are removed without documentation
Statistical tests are run manually
Graphs are exported separately

Six months later, a colleague asks:

“How did you exclude those patients?”

If the steps were not scripted, you may not know.
With reproducibility:

All exclusions are coded
All assumptions are documented
All outputs regenerate from the same script
The report updates automatically if data changes

The difference is clarity and control.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
section: Reproducibility Is Also an Ethical Issue
text:
Reproducibility Is Also an Ethical Issue
In healthcare, data analysis is not purely technical — it is ethical.
Transparent workflows:

Reduce unintentional bias
Prevent undocumented data manipulation
Make decisions defensible

Reproducibility demonstrates respect for the data and the people represented in it.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
text:
Building Reproducible Habits
You do not need complex systems to begin.
Start with:

Keeping raw data untouched
Writing cleaning steps in scripts (not manually)
Saving model code
Documenting assumptions clearly
Using Quarto or R Markdown to combine analysis and reporting

Small structural habits create large long-term stability.

title: Why Reproducibility Matters in Healthcare Data
text:
Final Thoughts
Healthcare data demands precision, transparency, and accountability.
Reproducibility is not about perfection. It is about responsibility.
When analysis is reproducible:

Results are trustworthy
Collaboration is smoother
Future updates are manageable
Decisions are defensible

And in healthcare, that matters.

text:
This project demonstrates a reproducible workflow for exploratory pharmacovigilance analysis using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) 2025 Q3 dataset.
Using structured R scripts and case-level aggregation, I examined:

Frequently reported adverse reaction terms
Case-level reporting patterns
Data structure and duplication considerations

This analysis is exploratory and intended for structured signal awareness rather than causal inference.
This case study reflects how I structure large healthcare datasets with clarity, traceability and cautious interpretation.

title: Reproducible Pharmacovigilance Workflow Using FAERS Data (2025 Q3)
text:
Analytical Objective
To examine reporting patterns in FAERS 2025 Q3 data by combining:
• Reaction reporting behaviour (REAC table)
• Outcome severity indicators (OUTC table)
The goal is exploratory signal awareness using case-level aggregation, not estimation of clinical risk.

title: Reproducible Pharmacovigilance Workflow Using FAERS Data (2025 Q3)
text:
Context
Spontaneous adverse event databases such as FAERS contain large volumes of real-world safety reports.
However, these data are frequently misinterpreted because reporting frequency is influenced by awareness, reporting behaviour, and follow-up submissions rather than true incidence.
For healthcare and research teams, the practical value of FAERS lies in structured signal awareness rather than causal inference.
This project explores how reporting patterns can be examined cautiously using a reproducible R workflow.

title: Reproducible Pharmacovigilance Workflow Using FAERS Data (2025 Q3)
text:
Data and Structural Consideration
It is important to note that FAERS data is based on spontaneous reports and does not represent confirmed adverse drug reactions.
Several limitations must be considered when interpreting FAERS adverse reaction data such as:

A single case may include multiple reported reactions
Reporting frequency does not equal incidence or risk
Duplicate or follow-up reports may exist
Reporting is influenced by media attention and regulatory actions

As a result, counts and trends should be interpreted cautiously and used for signal exploration rather than causal inference.
Important:
This analysis is exploratory and does not imply causality.
All analyses were conducted at the case level (caseid) to reduce over-counting from follow-up submissions.

title: Reproducible Pharmacovigilance Workflow Using FAERS Data (2025 Q3)
text:
Reproducible Workflow
To ensure traceability and repeatability, the analysis was performed using a scripted workflow in R rather than manual data manipulation.
The workflow consisted of:

Importing raw FAERS ASCII files directly into R
Performing case-level aggregation to avoid double counting follow-up reports
Applying cleaning and transformation steps through documented code
Generating tables and figures automatically from the analysis script

This approach ensures the results can be regenerated whenever the dataset is updated and provides a clear audit trail of all processing steps.

title: Reproducible Pharmacovigilance Workflow Using FAERS Data (2025 Q3)
text:
Analytical Approach
The analysis is structured in two complementary parts.
First, the REAC table is used to understand what types of reactions are most frequently reported and how reports are distributed across cases.
Second, the OUTC table is used to examine how serious those reported cases are.
Together, these perspectives allow cautious interpretation:
frequently reported events are not necessarily severe, and severe outcomes are not necessarily frequent.

text:
Interpretation
Combining reaction frequency and outcome severity provides a more cautious understanding of FAERS data.
Frequently reported reactions do not necessarily correspond to severe outcomes, and serious outcomes may occur in less frequently reported terms.
This demonstrates why spontaneous reporting databases should be used for signal awareness and prioritisation rather than risk estimation.

Clinical Context
It is very important to keep in mind that these are all real-life data with many missing values and errors. It is not possible to know where there may be errors, but a few possibilities include:

Error submitting an update as a new case
Entry error
Multiple drug administration by one patient leading to identifying the wrong drug as the culprit of adverse reactions

While there are many possible errors to keep in mind, the data has a huge number of cases reported. Larger reporting volume may reveal consistent patterns, but does not remove reporting bias. An increase in reports does not necessarily indicate increased risk. Possible contributions to the bias include:

Increased prescribing
Media attention
Regulatory changes

The results should be read and analysed with the potential errors and influences in mind, and any healthcare professionals or researchers who intend to use this as reference should always use their clinical judgement.


Key Findings

Reporting frequency is concentrated in a small subset of reaction terms
Most cases contain a limited number of reported reactions
Serious outcomes occur across both frequent and infrequent terms
Reaction frequency alone does not indicate clinical severity

title: Reproducible Pharmacovigilance Workflow Using FAERS Data (2025 Q3)
text:
Conclusion
This case study demonstrates a reproducible approach to structuring and interpreting large pharmacovigilance datasets in R.
By separating reaction frequency from outcome severity and analysing data at the case level, reporting patterns can be explored while maintaining appropriate clinical caution.
Such workflows support exploratory safety assessment and communication, but should not be interpreted as evidence of causality or incidence.
